title: Telnet Disabled
text: Telnet transmits all traffic, including credentials, in cleartext over the network. An attacker positioned on the network path (or performing ARP spoofing on a local segment) can passively capture administrative passwords and session content. Replace Telnet with SSH version 2 for all administrative access, and remove `transport input telnet` from VTY/console lines.

title: HTTP Management Disabled
text: Unencrypted HTTP management interfaces expose session cookies, credentials, and configuration data to network eavesdroppers. Disable the HTTP management service and require HTTPS (TLS) for any web-based device administration.

title: SSH Protocol Version 2
text: SSH protocol version 1 has known cryptographic weaknesses (weak integrity checks, vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks) and has been deprecated for over a decade. Configure devices to accept only SSH version 2.

title: Encrypted Management Enabled
text: Administrative sessions should always be encrypted end-to-end. Enabling HTTPS for web management and disabling plaintext protocols prevents credential and session-data interception on shared or compromised network segments.

title: Minimum Password Length
text: Short passwords are vulnerable to brute-force and dictionary attacks. Industry baselines (CIS, NIST 800-63B) recommend a minimum length of at least 8-14 characters depending on whether other compensating controls (MFA, lockout) are present.

title: Privileged Access Restricted
text: Weak or shared privileged-access mechanisms (e.g. a single shared enable password rather than per-user accountability) make it impossible to attribute administrative actions to an individual and increase the blast radius of a single credential compromise. Use per-user authentication with a strong, hashed enable secret rather than a plaintext enable password.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication
text: Passwords alone are vulnerable to phishing, credential stuffing, and keylogging. Multi-factor authentication significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized administrative access even if a password is compromised, where the platform supports it.

title: No Default Credential Indicators
text: Default or well-known vendor credentials (e.g. admin/admin, cisco/cisco) are the first thing attackers and automated scanners try. Any configuration containing such patterns should be treated as a critical, immediately actionable finding.

title: Logging Enabled
text: Without logging, there is no record of configuration changes, login attempts, or anomalous behavior, making incident detection and forensic investigation impossible. Device-level logging should always be enabled as a baseline control.

title: Remote Syslog Configured
text: Logs stored only locally on a device can be lost, rotated out, or deleted by an attacker who gains access. Forwarding logs to a centralized, access-controlled syslog server preserves an independent audit trail even if the device itself is later compromised.

title: Audit Logging Enabled
text: Accounting/audit logging (e.g. AAA accounting) records who performed which administrative commands and when, which is essential for accountability, compliance evidence, and post-incident review.

title: NTP Configured
text: Without a synchronized time source, log timestamps across devices cannot be reliably correlated during an investigation, which can make reconstructing an attack timeline impossible. Configure at least one trusted NTP source.

title: Secure SNMP Configuration
text: SNMP v1/v2c relies on community strings sent in cleartext with no real authentication, and default strings like 'public'/'private' are widely known. SNMPv3 provides authentication and encryption and should be used wherever SNMP is required.

title: No Unrestricted ACL Rules
text: An access-control rule that permits any-source to any-destination traffic effectively disables network segmentation, allowing lateral movement and negating the purpose of the control point. ACLs/firewall policies should follow least-privilege, permitting only the specific traffic that is required.

title: Management Plane Not Internet-Exposed
text: Exposing administrative interfaces (SSH, HTTP/S, Telnet) directly to the internet dramatically increases the attack surface, inviting credential-stuffing and exploit attempts from anywhere in the world. Management access should be restricted to trusted internal networks or a dedicated out-of-band management network/VPN.

title: No Insecure Services Enabled
text: Legacy or insecure services (Telnet, unauthenticated HTTP, etc.) that remain enabled by default on many platforms provide unnecessary attack surface with no corresponding benefit once modern secure alternatives are available.

title: No Unused Services Enabled
text: Services like Finger or BOOTP that are rarely needed in modern networks still consume resources and provide potential reconnaissance/attack vectors if left enabled. Disable any service that is not actively required.

title: Administrative Session Timeout
text: An administrative session with no inactivity timeout remains authenticated indefinitely if a workstation is left unattended, giving an opportunistic attacker persistent access. Configure a bounded idle timeout (commonly 10-15 minutes) on all management sessions.
